General.Description:
Naomi Flores was twenty-two years old and ranked seventh in the world in middle-distance running when the accident happened. She never describes the accident itself in this book. She says, simply and once: "The accident is not the story. What I did after it is."

What she did after it was, by any measure, remarkable. Eight months of rehabilitation. The decision — made alone, at four in the morning, in a hospital corridor — to compete in wheelchair racing. Three years of starting over in a sport she had to learn from the beginning while managing chronic pain, institutional indifference, and the well-meaning but crushing pity of people who saw a wheelchair before they saw an athlete. And then, at twenty-seven, a gold medal at the Paralympic Games in a world record time.

Unbreakable is the autobiography of someone who is ferociously honest about what recovery actually looks like — the backslides, the rage, the days when it is not possible to feel grateful for being alive — while never losing sight of the discipline and desire that pulled her through.

Flores writes with the same economy and precision she brings to racing. Not one word is wasted. Not one sentiment is false. This is the real thing.
